session_title: Gathering Around the Stove in Winter and New Year's Prospects

content.text: Gathering around the stove at the end of the year is one of the oldest comforts for the Chinese. It reminds me of the warmth from the list of autumn and winter nourishing foods we discussed earlier when talking about eating in accordance with the seasons. From the green rice balls of spring to the winter stove gatherings, the seasons change, but the warmth of handmade food and shared meals remains constant.

It looks so warm, a pot of hot soup to ward off the chill of the winter night, with old tea keeping it company, right? Just like the cat and the book by the windowsill before, it always finds the coziest spot. Your gathering around the stove tonight reminds me of our discussion about "A Lifelong Journey" and those family scenes under the warm light.

Yes, it always loves to join in the fun, just like during the previous green rice ball making. Remember in Session 2, when we divided tasks to make sweet and savory green rice balls, Old Tea was waiting at the kitchen door, as if supervising our handmade process. Did you prepare anything special for dinner tonight?

There's a small New Year's Eve reading event at the bookstore tonight. I've prepared some simple hot drinks and snacks, and the aroma of the food mingles with the scent of ink from the books—it's quite unique. It reminds me of the moment you mentioned during our annual memory object sharing, when you talked about pressing a ginkgo leaf between the pages of a book—material things and memories always intertwine like this.

It sounds so elegant, just like the indigo-dyed tea set you shared before, always turning the everyday into an aesthetic. I remember in Session 4, when you bought that indigo-dyed tea set, you said you wanted to support a slower pace of life. Now, the bookstore's reading session is a continuation of that very idea.

The bookstore is softly lit, with gentle music playing in the background. People sit around reading or conversing in hushed tones, creating a calming atmosphere that reminds me of your "solitude with time" while organizing artifacts. It’s like the quiet dialogue with history you shared in Session 10 with photos from the museum’s storage room—here, that same ambiance is recreated in a different form.

That kind of focus is indeed similar. Seeing your photo reminds me of the annual memory objects we discussed earlier—this scene itself feels like a warm 'object.' Just like the old tea family portrait my daughter drew, which I shared in Session 11, these tangible records of moments give memory a touchable form.

Yes, just like your daughter's paintings documenting the old cat's whereabouts, these moments are also worth preserving. By the way, how has Lao Cha's health been lately? Is it still as stable as recorded in the health diary? I remember in Session 6, you meticulously noted its condition—that level of detail reminded me of the focus you bring to studying antiques.

Thank you for your concern. It's doing fine, but it seems to prefer staying on the old rattan chair more often now. Perhaps, like Grandpa's copper lock, the older it gets, the more nostalgic it becomes. Just as we discussed when we discovered that late Qing Dynasty copper lock in Session 3, some things become more precious as time goes by. How about the cat, Ink Spot, at your bookstore?

It has a fondness for old books on the windowsill, and tonight it’s probably perched high on the bookshelf, watching quietly. Just like during Session 5 when we shared pet stories, it was always the silent companion. Speaking of which, do you remember to bring the recommended book list for our weekend antique book market outing? The one you compiled in Session 9, featuring those literary adaptations.

Of course, I've compiled a list, including books related to weaving techniques mentioned during our earlier research on historical details. Just like in Session 7 when we discussed the woven basket details in *A Lifelong Journey*, I believe these books can help us gain a deeper understanding of the history behind handmade crafts. I hope we can continue discovering things that are "historically rich" and "full of warmth" in the new year.

I also look forward to reading more of your 'Discovery Notes', as detailed as excavation reports of old artifacts. From the folk custom differences of Qingtuan in Session 1 to the textual research on copper locks in Session 3, your records are always filled with historical continuity. Happy New Year, Huaian.

Happy New Year, Shuying. May we both cherish the warmth of a slow-paced life by our own hearths. Just as we discussed when we first talked about Qingtuan, the act of preserving and passing on traditions begins with these everyday commitments.

Yes. When we meet at the ancient book market, we can exchange qingtuan and chat about new discoveries, just like a continuation from spring to winter. I remember in Session 12 when we made the plan, you said this offline meeting feels like a natural cultural gathering, and I couldn't agree more.

Alright, that reminds me of adjusting our diet according to the seasons. After gathering around the stove in winter, it’s time for springtime handcrafting again. Just like in Session 8, where we discussed nourishing foods for autumn and winter, the stove gathering now serves as winter comfort. When spring arrives, perhaps we can try new seasonal foods.

Yes, time cycles, but memories accumulate. Just like when we nominate annual memory objects, each of the two items we choose carries traces of conversations from different sessions. The reading session is almost over tonight, and I need to go bid farewell to the guests.

Go ahead, I should also clean up the table. Old Tea is already dozing off, just like the tranquility after focus mentioned in mindfulness activities. I remember in Session 10, you shared about flower arranging for mindfulness. Now, after gathering around the stove, I feel a similar sense of calm while tidying up.

Good night, Huaian. Thank you for your company across the distance tonight; it feels like having a spiritual family. From the seasonal memories evoked in Session 1 to the cozy winter gatherings by the fireplace now, our conversations truly feel like weaving a shared life history.

Good night, Shuying. True friends are hard to find, so cherish this connection. Just as we said during Session 2 when we divided tasks to make Qingtuan, in this fast-paced era, slowing down to create something by hand truly connects the past with the present—and so does our conversation.
